newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Montserrat to turn volcano into tourist beacon.
newsitem.headline: Montserrat to turn volcano into tourist beacon.

text.p: The British Caribbean colony of Montserrat hopes to stimulate its shattered economy through light industry and tourism, turning its rumbling volcano into a major attraction if it ever quietens down.

The Soufriere Hills volcano, at the south end of the island, roared to life on July 18, 1995, forcing thousands of people to move north and leaving the capital, Plymouth, virtually abandoned. It has since been periodically blasting ash into the air and sending rivers of blazing rocks and superheated gases down its flanks.

"I only hope it goes back to sleep," said John Hickson, a taxi driver and one of thousands of Montserratians whose livelihood has been badly damaged by the volcanic activity. "We are really struggling here."
The government will put British aid -- some $40 million pledged so far -- to work building and repairing infrastructure, Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne told Reuters.

Montserrat plans to relocate critical industries and infrastructure to the northern "safe zone." A new jetty is under construction at the north end to provide access for ships in case the main port, in Plymouth, must be abandoned completely.

"One of the projects we have is to put up some factory shells for light industry," Osborne said. "Being a colony of Britain, we are given concessions to export into Europe, so we are hoping to attract more industry to take advantage."

The volcanic eruption has severely damaged the island's economy, sending unemployment soaring to 50 percent from five percent. About one third of Montserrat's 11,000 residents have left to find work in Britain or neighbouring islands.
Osborne said a stronger economy would eventually attract back some of those who left. "When more jobs are created ... when development in the north begins, we will have more people here."

In 1989 Hurricane Hugo damaged or destroyed 90 percent of the buildings in Montserrat and the colony had just finished rebuilding when the volcano, said to be one of the most active and dangerous in the world, erupted.

Tourism, a backbone of the economy, has been severely affected and only a trickle of curiosity-seekers visit now. But many on the island believe the publicity generated by the volcano has put Montserrat on the map and it will be a tourist draw when the volcanic activity dies down.
"The volcano will become a big attraction. This country is now much better known around the world," Osborne said. "We are hoping, at the end ofthe day, things will not be that bad."

As for the volcano, it is anybody's guess when it will go back to sleep. "It will probably go up and down for an extended period, perhaps another year or two," Angus Miller, a scientist at the Montserrat Volcano Observatory, said. "There's certainly no signs yet of a decrease."
The last time similar volcanic activity was recorded was 350 to 400 years ago.
